candidates.scenario: Pay-or-quit includes late fee
candidates.facts: Landlord serves a 3-day notice to pay rent or quit on a month-to-month residential tenant. The notice demands $1,800 in unpaid rent plus a $150 late fee, for a total of $1,950. The lease provides for a $150 late fee. The tenant has not paid rent for one month.
candidates.question: Is the notice legally sufficient under CCP §1161(2)?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: A 3-day pay-or-quit notice that demands any amount beyond unpaid rent (including late fees) overstates the amount owed and voids the notice under CCP §1161(2). See Orozco v. Casimiro, 121 Cal. App. 4th Supp. 7 (2004). The defect is not curable by amendment.
candidates.edge_cases: What if the late fee is separately listed but notice says 'landlord may choose to waive'? DRAFT: still void — overstated amount on face.

candidates.scenario: Pay-or-quit for exact rent only
candidates.facts: Landlord serves a 3-day notice to pay rent or quit demanding exactly $2,000 — the tenant's monthly rent. No late fees or utilities are included. Tenant is month-to-month, tenancy 8 months.
candidates.question: Is the notice legally sufficient under CCP §1161(2)?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: The notice demands only unpaid rent, the correct amount. No overstatement. Proper notice type for nonpayment. 3-day period complies with CCP §1161(2).
candidates.edge_cases: If tenant tenders exact amount within 3 days, landlord must accept or waive breach.

candidates.scenario: 30-day notice to long-term tenant (>12 months)
candidates.facts: Landlord serves a 30-day notice to terminate tenancy on a month-to-month residential tenant who has resided at the property for 18 months. The property is not exempt from AB 1482 (a multi-family building, built 2010, more than 10 years from notice date).
candidates.question: Is the 30-day notice period sufficient?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: A tenant who has continuously resided at the property for 12 months or more requires a 60-day notice under CCP §1946.1(b). A 30-day notice is insufficient and voids the termination.
candidates.edge_cases: If the unit is exempt from AB 1482 (e.g., single-family home with proper notice of exemption), the notice period requirement still applies — §1946.1 is separate from AB 1482 just-cause.

candidates.scenario: 60-day notice to short-term tenant (<12 months)
candidates.facts: Landlord serves a 60-day notice to terminate tenancy on a month-to-month residential tenant of 9 months. The property is a multi-family building not exempt from AB 1482.
candidates.question: Is the 60-day notice period sufficient?
candidates.DRAFT_answer: YES — valid as to notice period
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Tenant has resided fewer than 12 months, so 30-day minimum applies under CCP §1946.1(b). A 60-day notice exceeds the minimum and is sufficient as to period. Note: AB 1482 just-cause analysis is separate and would also need to be evaluated.
candidates.edge_cases: Notice period is valid; AB 1482 just-cause requirement is a separate issue not tested here.

candidates.scenario: Cure-or-quit for unauthorized pet (curable)
candidates.facts: Landlord serves a 3-day notice to cure or quit to a tenant who has an unauthorized dog in violation of the lease. The notice specifies the violation and gives the tenant 3 days to remove the dog. The lease prohibits pets.
candidates.question: Is this the correct notice type and is the notice period sufficient?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: An unauthorized pet is a curable lease violation. CCP §1161(3) requires a 3-day cure-or-quit for curable violations. The notice correctly identifies the violation and gives the tenant the opportunity to cure. An unconditional quit would be improper for a first curable violation.
candidates.edge_cases: If tenant already cured an identical violation once, some courts treat repeated violation as incurable. DRAFT: first violation = curable.

candidates.scenario: Unconditional quit for first unauthorized pet (no cure option)
candidates.facts: Landlord serves a 3-day unconditional notice to quit (no cure option) to a tenant who has an unauthorized dog in violation of the lease. This is the first such violation.
candidates.question: Is the notice type correct?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: A first-time curable lease violation requires a cure-or-quit notice under CCP §1161(3). An unconditional quit notice for an ongoing curable violation (where cure is possible) deprives the tenant of the statutory right to cure and voids the notice.
candidates.edge_cases: If the lease has been violated in the same way previously and tenant was warned or prior notice was served, DRAFT: may be incurable as repeated violation — flag for attorney.

candidates.scenario: No-cause termination on AB 1482-covered tenant
candidates.facts: Landlord serves a 60-day no-cause termination notice on a residential tenant who has lived in the unit for 3 years. The unit is in a multi-family building constructed in 2010 (more than 10 years ago). Tenant has not received any notice that the unit is exempt from AB 1482. No just cause is stated.
candidates.question: Is the notice valid?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: The unit is covered by AB 1482 (Civ. Code §1946.2): multi-family, >15 years old, no exempt status. The tenant has continuously resided for 12+ months. A no-cause termination notice is void because AB 1482 requires just cause to evict a qualifying tenant. The notice must state one of the enumerated just-cause grounds.
candidates.edge_cases: If landlord provided AB 1482 exemption notice at lease signing for a qualifying exempt property, analysis changes.

candidates.scenario: No-cause termination in AB 1482 exempt single-family home
candidates.facts: Landlord owns a single-family home. At the start of the tenancy, landlord provided written notice that the property is exempt from AB 1482 under Civ. Code §1946.2(e)(8) (single-family residence with proper written exemption notice). Landlord now serves a 60-day no-cause termination on a 3-year tenant.
candidates.question: Is the notice valid as to AB 1482?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Owner-occupied single-family residences and separately alienable single-family homes where written exemption notice was provided at or before commencement of tenancy are exempt from AB 1482 just-cause requirements under Civ. Code §1946.2(e)(8). Notice period must still comply with CCP §1946.1 (60 days for 12+ month tenant — satisfied here).
candidates.edge_cases: If exemption notice was not provided at lease signing or renewal, exemption does not apply even for SFR. Verify written notice was actually given.

candidates.scenario: Pay-or-quit includes utilities listed as additional rent in lease
candidates.facts: Lease requires tenant to pay $1,800/month base rent plus $100/month water/trash as 'additional rent.' Landlord serves 3-day notice demanding $1,900 (base + utilities). Lease language: 'monthly rent is $1,800 plus $100 additional rent for water/trash service.'
candidates.question: Does including the $100 utilities overstate the notice amount?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: If utilities are contractually defined as 'additional rent' in the lease, including them may be permissible under CCP §1161(2) (which allows demand for 'rent due'). However, courts have reached different results depending on whether 'additional rent' language is sufficiently specific. DRAFT: likely valid if utilities are designated as additional rent in the lease, but this is a frequent litigation point.
candidates.edge_cases: Distinction: contractually-designated 'additional rent' vs. separately-charged fees not part of the rent obligation. This is the core uncertainty.

candidates.scenario: Notice served for rent already partially paid
candidates.facts: Tenant owes $2,400 in back rent ($1,200 x 2 months). Tenant pays $1,200 before landlord serves notice. Landlord serves 3-day notice for $2,400 (full pre-payment amount), not the remaining $1,200.
candidates.question: Is the notice valid?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: The notice overstates the amount owed at the time of service. At the time the notice was served, only $1,200 remained unpaid. Demanding $2,400 — more than actually owed — voids the notice under the overstatement rule. See Levitz Furniture Co. v. Wingtip Communications (2001); CCP §1161(2).
candidates.edge_cases: If landlord re-serves a corrected notice for $1,200, that new notice starts a new 3-day period.

candidates.scenario: 3-day notice: period calculated from service date vs. next day
candidates.facts: Landlord personally serves a 3-day pay-or-quit notice on Monday. Tenant tenders full rent on Thursday (3 days after service). Landlord refuses tender and files UD on Thursday.
candidates.question: Did tenant cure within the 3-day period?
candidates.DRAFT_answer: YES — within period (but verify court rules on calculation)
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Under CCP §1161, the 3-day period begins the day after service (Monday = day 0; Tuesday = day 1; Wednesday = day 2; Thursday = day 3). Thursday tender is within the period. UD filed on day 3 before expiration is premature. However: courts split on whether weekends extend the period under CCP §12a — flag for attorney.
candidates.edge_cases: Weekend/holiday extension under CCP §12a if day 3 falls on weekend. Attorney should establish the correct computation rule.

candidates.scenario: Notice missing tenant's name
candidates.facts: Landlord serves a 3-day notice to pay or quit that identifies the unit by address but does not name the tenant (addressed only to 'All Occupants'). The actual tenant is a named individual who signed the lease.
candidates.question: Is the omission of the tenant's name a fatal defect?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Courts have generally required that a UD notice adequately identify the party being noticed. 'All Occupants' may be sufficient to include unnamed occupants, but a named lessee not identified by name may have grounds to challenge the notice. Outcome varies by court. DRAFT: likely challengeable defect but not universally void.
candidates.edge_cases: Different result if tenant goes by a different name / lease is in different name.

candidates.scenario: Cure-or-quit: tenant cures within period, landlord proceeds anyway
candidates.facts: Landlord serves 3-day cure-or-quit for unauthorized subletting. Tenant vacates the subtenant within 2 days. Landlord files UD on day 4, claiming the breach was incurable.
candidates.question: Is the UD action sustainable?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: If the violation was curable (unauthorized subletting is typically curable on first offense) and tenant cured within the 3-day period, the notice is satisfied and landlord's UD cause of action has not ripened. Landlord must allege and prove failure to cure. Timely cure defeats the UD.
candidates.edge_cases: If subtenancy had been ongoing for extended period, some courts may treat as incurable. DRAFT: first-offense sublet = curable.

candidates.scenario: Just-cause termination: owner move-in (AB 1482 covered unit)
candidates.facts: Landlord owns a 4-unit building built in 2005 (21 years old). Tenant has been there 2 years. Landlord serves 60-day termination notice stating 'owner intends to occupy the unit as primary residence' under Civ. Code §1946.2(b)(2)(A).
candidates.question: Is owner move-in a valid just cause under AB 1482?
candidates.DRAFT_answer: YES — valid just cause if owner complies with all requirements
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Owner move-in is an enumerated no-fault just cause under Civ. Code §1946.2(b)(2)(A). Requirements: (1) landlord or qualifying family member must genuinely intend to occupy; (2) relocation assistance equal to one month's rent must be paid; (3) if unit is not occupied within 90 days, tenant has right of first refusal. Notice must state these conditions.
candidates.edge_cases: Failure to pay relocation assistance, or failure to actually move in, may defeat the just cause and expose landlord to penalties.

candidates.scenario: Retaliation defense — notice served within 180 days of tenant complaint
candidates.facts: Tenant complained to the local housing department about habitability conditions on March 1. Landlord serves a 3-day pay-or-quit notice on April 15 (45 days later) for nonpayment of rent. Rent was actually owed for the prior month.
candidates.question: Does the timing create a rebuttable presumption of retaliation under Civ. Code §1942.5?
candidates.DRAFT_answer: YES — presumption of retaliation arises; landlord must rebut
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Civ. Code §1942.5(a) creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliatory eviction if a notice to terminate (including pay-or-quit) is served within 180 days of a protected tenant activity (here, housing complaint). Landlord can rebut by showing a legitimate non-retaliatory reason. Note: this is a defense to a UD, not a defect that voids the notice on its face — but tenant may assert it in UD proceedings.
candidates.edge_cases: Rent was actually owed — landlord has a legitimate non-retaliatory reason. Rebuttable, not conclusive. Outcome depends on trier of fact.

candidates.scenario: Waiver: landlord accepts rent after serving notice
candidates.facts: Landlord serves a 3-day pay-or-quit notice. On day 2, landlord accepts a partial payment of $500 (tenant owed $2,000). Landlord then proceeds with UD after the notice period expires.
candidates.question: Does acceptance of partial payment waive the notice?
candidates.DRAFT_answer: YES — waiver; notice must be re-served
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Acceptance of any payment after serving a pay-or-quit notice waives the notice under California UD law. The landlord's right to enforce the notice is extinguished. If the remaining rent is still unpaid, landlord must serve a new notice for the outstanding amount. Partial acceptance cannot be conditioned on 'without prejudice' reservation in most CA UD contexts.
candidates.edge_cases: Some leases include 'acceptance of partial payment is not a waiver' clauses. DRAFT: under CA residential UD law, such clauses are generally unenforceable for pre-service payments but courts split post-notice — flag for attorney.

candidates.scenario: Notice served on subtenant who is not named in the head lease
candidates.facts: The named tenant (A) sublet to B without authorization. Landlord knows B is occupying and serves the 3-day notice only on A (not on B). A is not present at the property.
candidates.question: Is notice valid as to unnamed subtenant B?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: A UD action must name all parties against whom possession is sought. An unlawful subtenant may need to be served separately, or may be named as 'Doe' occupant. Failure to serve or name B may allow B to remain in possession even if A is evicted. DRAFT: to be safe, name and serve all known occupants.
candidates.authority: CCP §1161; CCP §415.46 (prejudgment claim of right to possession)
candidates.edge_cases: Prejudgment Claim of Right to Possession process allows unnamed occupants to be bound. Attorney should advise on process.

candidates.scenario: Pay-or-quit: amount includes prospective rent not yet due
candidates.facts: Tenant is behind on two months of rent ($2,400). The 3-day notice demands $3,600 — two months past due plus one month upcoming.
candidates.question: Is the notice valid?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: A pay-or-quit notice may only demand rent actually owed (past due) at the time of service. Prospective rent not yet due cannot be included. Demanding $3,600 overstates the obligation owed at service and voids the notice.
candidates.edge_cases: If additional month becomes due before the 3 days expire, tenant may owe it — but the notice still demands an incorrect amount at service and is void.

candidates.scenario: 3-day notice: unit subject to local rent ordinance with stricter just-cause requirements
candidates.facts: Landlord owns a unit in the City of Los Angeles. Tenant has resided there for 4 years. Landlord serves a 3-day pay-or-quit for nonpayment. The unit is covered by the LA RSO (Rent Stabilization Ordinance). Rent was genuinely unpaid.
candidates.question: Is the 3-day pay-or-quit valid despite RSO coverage?
candidates.DRAFT_answer: YES — nonpayment is permitted just cause under LA RSO
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: Nonpayment of rent is an enumerated just cause for eviction under LAMC §151.09(A)(1). A 3-day pay-or-quit for genuine nonpayment complies with both state law (CCP §1161) and local RSO. The RSO restricts no-cause evictions but does not protect tenants from nonpayment terminations.
candidates.edge_cases: Los Angeles has additional COVID-era protections and local notice requirements. Attorney should verify current LAMC provisions — this DRAFT reflects general RSO framework.

candidates.scenario: Cure-or-quit: violation is incurable by nature (damage to unit)
candidates.facts: Tenant caused significant damage to the unit by removing load-bearing wall (structural modification). Landlord serves a 3-day cure-or-quit. Damage cannot be repaired in 3 days.
candidates.question: Should a cure-or-quit or unconditional quit be served?
candidates.DRAFT_reasoning: For violations that are physically impossible to cure within the notice period, courts have held that a cure-or-quit may be treated as an unconditional quit in effect. However, some courts require an unconditional quit notice for incurable breaches (CCP §1161(4) covers deliberate and substantial damage). DRAFT: unconditional quit under §1161(4) may be the correct notice type — flag for attorney.
candidates.edge_cases: If the damage was intentional/malicious, §1161(4) (material and willful breach) applies and an unconditional quit is appropriate.
